title: Peripheral edema associated with calcium channel blockers: incidence and withdrawal rate--a meta-analysis of randomized trials
authors: Makani H, Bangalore S, Romero J, Htyte N, Berrios RS, Makwana H, et al.
population: 106 randomised trials in hypertension, published 1980 to January 2011, with at least 100 patients in the calcium channel blocker arm; mean age 56 years
funder: not read: the publisher page is not accessible, and PubMed and Europe PMC list no grants.
result: Weighted incidence of peripheral oedema 10.7% with calcium channel blockers against 3.2% with control or placebo (P<0.0001); withdrawal because of oedema 2.1% against 0.5%. Both rose with duration of therapy, reaching 24% and 5% after 6 months. Dihydropyridines 12.3% against non-dihydropyridines 3.1%; high doses (more than half the usual maximal dose) 16.1% against low doses 5.7%; lipophilic dihydropyridines relative risk 0.43 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.53) against traditional dihydropyridines. The authors state that oedema has been thought to arise from arteriolar dilatation causing intracapillary hypertension and fluid extravasation.
